feedback: If your measured third side or remaining angles differ noticeably from about 6.7 cm, 47° and 78°, do not accept them as 'close enough'. This is evidence of accumulated error: recheck the protractor centre on the vertex, the zero-line along the side, and which scale you read
If you set 125° where 55° was asked, you read the wrong scale and drew the supplement; re-estimate 'bigger or smaller than a square corner?' and pick the scale that agrees

If the sides or angle drift from 6 cm / 8 cm / 55°, rehearse the base-then-included-angle-then-side sequence on another figure. Use the self-check of measuring the third side and the remaining angles against their expected values
activities.intendedInsight: Accurate construction depends on a disciplined sequence (base → included angle → side → join the endpoints) and on choosing the right scale on a dual-scale protractor by first estimating against a right angle. Joining the endpoints always closes an SAS triangle, so accuracy is checked by comparing the measured third side (about 6.7 cm) and remaining angles (about 47° and 78°) with the expected values, not by whether the triangle closes.
learnerActions: Construct a triangle from two sides of 6 cm and 8 cm with an included angle of 55° between them: rule the first side from the ruler's zero, place the protractor with its centre on the endpoint vertex and zero-line along the side, set the 55° angle, measure and mark the second side, then rule the third side to close the triangle

Before reading the protractor, estimate first: 'Is 55° bigger or smaller than a right angle (a square corner)?' Smaller, so choose the scale that gives a value under 90°, not the 125° on the other scale

Because you finish by joining the two free endpoints, an SAS triangle always closes, so closing does not show it is accurate. Instead, measure the third side and the other two angles and compare them with the expected values. For 6 cm, 8 cm and 55°, the third side should be about 6.7 cm and the other angles about 47° and 78°, and all three angles add up to 180°. A clear mismatch signals placement or measurement error: recheck the vertex placement, the zero-line and the scale you chose
Aim for accuracy to about the nearest degree and nearest millimetre
activities.title: SAS construction with the estimate-first protractor routine

feedback: If you picked the additive option (6.5 m), recall that each 1 cm represents 2 m, so the relationship multiplies: 4.5 × 2 = 9 m
If you picked the answer with no units, remember the real length is in metres (9 m)
For the scale item, estimate the angle against a right angle first, then pick the agreeing scale
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising additive and units-dropped distractors and choosing the correct protractor scale reinforces the multiplicative structure and the estimate-first habit; recognising the right answer among options is not the same as independently constructing or converting, so this consolidates rather than replaces the full task.
learnerActions: Answer a conversion item such as: a wall measures 4.5 cm on a plan at 1 cm : 2 m — what is the real length? Choose from options that include an additive distractor (6.5 m from adding) and a units-dropped distractor ('9' with no units) alongside the correct 9 m
Answer a 'which scale reads this angle?' item: given an angle estimated smaller than a right angle, decide which of the two protractor scales to read
Explain in words why you multiply rather than add, and why the units matter
activities.title: Check scale reasoning and protractor scale choice (recognition practice)
